items.text: Through this project, we’ve developed ten research prototype interfaces and conducted usability studies with 300+ participants and real-world users showing improved reading experiences for scholars.
items.why: Claims evaluation results across prototypes that invite scrutiny of methodology and user selection.
items.plain: We created ten research prototype interfaces and evaluated them with over 300 participants and real-world users, demonstrating that they improved reading experiences for scholars.

items.text: Based on lab and field studies, CiteSee showed promise that providing visual augmentation and personalized context around inline citations in an interactive reading environment can allow readers to more effectively discover relevant prior work and keep track of their exploration during real-world literature review tasks.
items.why: Claims user study results for CiteSee that require evaluating study setup and scope.
items.plain: In laboratory and field evaluations, CiteSee showed potential to help readers discover relevant prior work and track their progress during real-world literature reviews by providing visual highlights and personalized context for inline citations.

items.text: In a lab study, CiteRead helped readers better understand a research paper and its follow-on work compared to providing readers with a separate interface for faceted browsing of follow-on work.
items.why: Claims superior performance over a baseline interface in a laboratory study.
items.plain: In a laboratory evaluation, CiteRead helped readers better understand a paper and its follow-on work compared to using a separate interface for faceted browsing of follow-on work.

items.text: Usability studies of Scim have shown these highlights can reduce the time it takes readers to find specific information within a paper.
items.why: Claims a specific usability outcome for Scim highlights that needs reader verification.
items.plain: Usability evaluations showed that Scim's highlights reduced the time required for readers to locate specific information in a paper.

items.text: An exploratory field deployment study with mixed-ability groups of low-vision and sighted readers revealed that readers found value in creating and consuming these links, and that reader-created links can increase trust.
items.why: Claims positive findings from an exploratory field deployment of Ocean.
items.plain: An exploratory field deployment with low-vision and sighted readers showed that participants valued creating and using these links, and that reader-created links can increase trust.

items.text: In a usability study, the above interactions reduced the time it took readers to find answers to questions involving the understanding of terminology.
items.why: Claims quantitative speed improvements and subjective satisfaction in a ScholarPhi usability study.
items.plain: In a usability study, these interactions reduced the time readers needed to answer questions about terminology, and all readers reported they would frequently or always use the tooltips and formula diagrams if available in their PDF readers.

items.text: In a usability study, readers made more frequent use of passage summaries than definition tooltips when both were available, suggesting the potential value of plain language summaries as allowing readers to bypass definitions of individual terms when acquiring a broad understanding of a paper.
items.why: Reports relative user behavior preferences observed during a Paper Plain usability study.
items.plain: In a usability study where both were available, readers used passage summaries more often than definition tooltips, suggesting plain language summaries can help readers get a broad understanding without reading individual definitions.

items.text: Our early-stage evaluations of Papeo suggest that readers can use these interactions to fluidly transition between watching video and reading text, using video to quickly understand, and then selectively descending into the text when they desire a detailed understanding of the paper.
items.why: Claims early-stage evaluation results for Papeo based on user interactions.
items.plain: Our early evaluations of Papeo indicate that readers can fluidly transition between watching video and reading text to gain a quick understanding before reading detailed text.

items.text: A lab study showed that Threddy was able to lower the interaction costs of saving clips while maintaining context, allowed participants to curate research threads without breaking reading flows, and discover interesting new papers to further grow their understanding of the research fields.
items.why: Claims positive user study outcomes for Threddy that invite evaluation.
items.plain: A laboratory study demonstrated that Threddy lowered the interaction costs of saving clips while preserving context, allowed participants to curate research threads without interrupting reading, and helped them discover new papers.

items.text: A usability study comparing Relatedly to a strong document-centric baseline showed that Relatedly led to participants writing summaries that were rated significantly more coherent, insightful, and detailed after 20 minutes of literature review.
items.why: Claims statistically significant superiority over a document-centric baseline in literature review output.
items.plain: In a usability study comparing Relatedly to a strong document-centric baseline, participants using Relatedly wrote literature review summaries rated as significantly more coherent, insightful, and detailed after 20 minutes.

items.text: The SciA11y system6 demonstrates this approach, automatically converting 12M academic PDFs to HTML [97]; a user study with blind and low vision participants demonstrated strong user appreciation of the output, though some errors remain (e.g., failing in certain cases to distinguish footnotes from body text, difficulty parsing math equations) [98].
items.why: Reports conversion metrics and user evaluation findings alongside specific parsing failures for SciA11y.
items.plain: The SciA11y system automatically converted 12 million academic PDFs to HTML, and a user study with blind and low-vision participants showed high user appreciation despite errors like misidentifying footnotes as body text or failing to parse math equations.

items.text: The bar for deploying AI models to support real-world reading is high; we often found during iterative design and usability studies that even slight errors in these models can have detrimental effects on the readers.
items.why: States a system limitation regarding user sensitivity to small AI model errors.
items.plain: Deploying AI models for real-world reading requires high accuracy, as iterative design and usability studies showed that even minor model errors can harm reader experiences.

items.text: While recent work has shown that these models can occasionally make critical errors or generate factually incorrect text when processing scientific text [72], we remain cautiously optimistic about developing ways to address their limitations [25, 55].
items.why: Acknowledges fundamental failure modes of large language models on scientific text.
items.plain: Large language models can occasionally make critical errors or generate factually incorrect content when processing scientific text.

items.text: For instance, using signals such as citation counts faces the risk of a “rich get richer” bias, which can reflect other kinds of documented biases [3, 64, 101].
items.why: Identifies a threat to validity regarding algorithmic selection bias.
items.plain: Using signals like citation counts creates a risk of "rich get richer" bias that can reinforce existing documented biases.

items.text: A related issue is around systems for more efficient reading or synthesis, which may encourage readers to take shortcuts that lead to incorrect understanding, sloppy research, or even outright plagiarism.
items.why: States a risk that efficiency tools might promote superficial reading and poor research habits.
items.plain: Systems designed for faster reading or synthesis might lead readers to take shortcuts that result in incorrect understanding, careless research, or plagiarism.

items.text: Validating our approach of augmenting existing PDFs of research papers, we have seen tremendous adoption of the freely-available Semantic Reader product1 which has grown to 10k weekly users.7 While we focused on augmenting PDF documents to support common scholar reading practices, all of our reading interfaces are built with web technologies—allowing these novel interactions to extend to future publication formats which can be rendered in web browsers.
items.why: Claims deployment scale metrics for the production system.
items.plain: The freely available Semantic Reader product has grown to 10,000 weekly users.
